newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Woman forcibly circumcised by Sierre Leon cult.
newsitem.headline: Woman forcibly circumcised by Sierre Leon cult.

text.p: A 28-year-old Sierra Leone woman said she was forcibly circumcised by a female cult gang who accused her of spying on them.
Daphne Pratt, a Krio (Creole), told Reuters she was seized at night two months ago by members of the powerful Bondo secret society that defends female circumcision.
"The women accused me of spying on their activities," Pratt said. "They said...it was we the Krio who were causing all their problems by publicising their traditions."
"Then they said they would teach me a lesson, and several of them threw me down on the ground. Then they tore off my pants and with a blade started slicing..." she said at a doctor's clinic.
When she came to, she managed to reach her uncle's house who took her to a police station.

"They (police) said it was a tribal matter and that I should go to a tribal court. Until now no one has got involved because they all say it is a politically sensitive issue," said Pratt, who termed herself a devout Christian.
"Daphne needed 15 stitches and a blood transfusion," said a gynaecologist who treated her and asked not to be identified for fear of reprisal. "She had to be hospitalised for almost a month."

In Sierra Leone, female secret societies, especially the Bondo, have come under the spotlight over female circumcision -- termed genital mutilation by opponents -- which is generally a preliminary rite for training girls for womanhood.

Medical workers have stepped up a campaign to draw attention to hazards of the practice, which affects about 90 percent of Sierra Leone women. Hundreds of Bondo women marched in Freetown in September to protest against that campaign.

Female circumcision is defended by traditional societes on various grounds, such as hygiene and curbing promiscuity by denying the woman sexual pleasure. By implication, circumcision should increase a woman's chances of getting a husband.
